subject: Ronaldinho — the post-Barcelona career (Milan, Flamengo, Atlético Mineiro, Querétaro, 2008–2015)
thesis: We pity Ronaldinho's post-Barcelona career. Ronaldinho doesn't. He won the Copa Libertadores at 33, took a Mexican club to its first ever Liga MX final at 35, and made the Estadio Azteca cry. The seven 'lost years' weren't lost. They were just played in leagues we'd decided not to watch — and the trophies he won there were heavier than most of what his peers won in the leagues we did. The pity tells us more about us than him.
title: The Trophies Ronaldinho Won After You Stopped Watching
hook: Between 2008 and 2015, football wrote off Ronaldinho. In those same seven years he won the Copa Libertadores at 33, took Querétaro to a Liga MX final, and made the Azteca crowd cry. We pity his lost years. He doesn't. The pity is ours.

chapters.beat: Cold open: ~12s of Brazilian commentator screaming as Ronaldinho lifts the 2013 Copa Libertadores trophy at the Mineirão. Then narrator over BLACK with the thesis question. Total cold-open ~55s.
chapters.narration:
In July twenty thirteen, this man lifted the Copa Libertadores. South America's biggest trophy. The hardest cup in club football to win. He was thirty-three years old. He had spent the previous five years being told, by almost everyone watching the sport, that he was finished.

He wasn't finished. He just wasn't playing in front of you anymore.

Between two thousand and eight and two thousand and fifteen — the seven-year period football media collectively designated ron-al-DEEN-yo's decline — he won eight major trophies, on three continents, in front of audiences nobody in Europe was watching. This video is the story of those seven years. Of a player generally agreed to be finished who, in fact, never was.

The question this video is built around is not what was wrong with ron-al-DEEN-yo's later career.

The question is what was wrong with us.

chapters.title: They Stopped Watching
chapters.beat: Milan, summer 2008. Free transfer. Pep prefers Messi. Real, City, Milan. The 'graceful sideways' framing. 10 goals year one. Ancelotti's 'very precarious' line. The 2009-10 recovery (top assister Serie A, 15 goals) under Allegri — credit goes to Milan, not him. Ibrahimović + Robinho + Cassano arrive. Allegri's '2am' line. Departs January 2011. Like ask embedded at end.
chapters.narration:
Milan, summer of two thousand and eight.

ron-al-DEEN-yo arrives at the San Siro on a free transfer. He has spent the previous twelve months in a war of attrition with Pep Guardiola, who has just taken over at Barcelona and decided, correctly, that he prefers Lionel Messi at number ten and ron-al-DEEN-yo not at all. Real Madrid have considered him. Manchester City — newly oil-money, hungry for a name — have offered a fortune. He chooses Milan.

The Italian press present this as a graceful step. Milan have just won the Champions League, the year before, under Carlo ahn-cheh-LOT-tee. They are not a step down. They are a sideways move into a different colour.

Then ron-al-DEEN-yo plays.

He scores ten in his first season. By his standards, ten is bad. By Milan's standards, ten is bad. By Italian football's standards in two thousand and eight, ten is mediocre. The Italian press, which has spent the autumn writing odes, switches to writing autopsies before December. ahn-cheh-LOT-tee, asked at a press conference in February whether ron-al-DEEN-yo's level can return, says — and this is the public record — that his physical condition is, in his exact phrasing, 'very precarious.'

Very precarious. From the coach. About a thirty-year-old who has won everything in the sport.

What ahn-cheh-LOT-tee meant, the journalists in the room understood. ron-al-DEEN-yo's training-ground attendance was, by every account from inside the club, complicated. He arrived. He was charming. He was technically still capable of producing the moments he was famous for. He was also, after most of the evenings he was supposed to be resting, somewhere else. The English football writer Jonathan Wilson would later put it cleanly: at Milan, ron-al-DEEN-yo had become a part-time genius.

The two-thousand-nine-to-ten season was, briefly, his recovery. ahn-cheh-LOT-tee left for Chelsea. Massimiliano ah-LEH-gree took over. ron-al-DEEN-yo finished the season as Serie A's leading assister. He scored fifteen goals. By any honest reading, the second-best player in the league behind Diego Milito.

The football media, by then, had stopped grading him on a curve. The coverage of two-thousand-nine-to-ten was not 'ron-al-DEEN-yo recovers.' The coverage was 'Milan look better.' The credit went to the manager. The credit went to the system. The credit went to the new signings around him. The man producing the assists got mentioned the way you mention a piece of furniture that hasn't broken.

The third season, Zlatan Ibrahimović arrived. Then ho-BEEN-yo. Then Antonio kah-SAH-no. ron-al-DEEN-yo started fewer than half of Milan's matches in the autumn. In November, ah-LEH-gree was photographed in a press conference saying, of his own player, that 'it's not the hour for an athlete to still be awake.' He had been seen, days before a Milan derby, leaving a Milanese bar at two in the morning.

By January, ron-al-DEEN-yo was in negotiations to leave. By the end of the same January window, he had signed for Flamengo.

He was thirty years old.

The global football press wrote his obituary that month. The same press had been writing it, on and off, since he first arrived at the San Siro. The press was, at that moment, not entirely wrong. The Milan years were not what they should have been. He was, by his own previous standards, a partial player.

What the press got wrong was the assumption that the partial player was the final version.

If you forgot ron-al-DEEN-yo was even still playing in twenty-eleven, drop a like. That's basically the whole point of this video — and the algorithm only pushes it to the next person if it knows you're still here.

chapters.title: He Went Home
chapters.beat: January 2011. Flamengo unveiling at Maracanã, 50K people. Boavista free kick. The 5-4 Santos comeback (3-0 down, hat-trick + 2 assists, Neymar dismissed in the press). 35 goals / 58 apps for Flamengo. May 2012, contractual dispute, leaves. Four days later: Atlético Mineiro. 2012 Brasileirão second place. Bola de Ouro 2012. The Guardian / Marca two-paragraphs treatment.
chapters.narration:
Rio de Janeiro, January two thousand and eleven. Flamengo unveil their new signing in front of fifty thousand people.

The press conference is conducted from a stage in the centre of the Maracanã. The shirt — the famous red and black — is held up by ron-al-DEEN-yo with both hands. The pose is identical to the pose he held on signing for Barcelona seven years earlier. The difference is the audience. In Barcelona, he had been signing for one of the largest sporting institutions on Earth. In Rio, he was signing for a Brazilian first-division club whose European broadcast deal was, charitably, rounding error.

This was, by the football media's calculation, the formal beginning of his retirement. A homecoming. A nostalgia move. The legacy lap before the boots came off.

Then, again, ron-al-DEEN-yo played.

In his first month, against Boavista in the Carioca championship, he stood over a free kick from twenty-five yards and curled a ball into the corner of the net so cleanly the Brazilian commentator on the broadcast — a man who had presumably narrated thousands of free kicks — broke into laughter mid-call. Flamengo went on to win that trophy. The first piece of silverware ron-al-DEEN-yo had won since his last full season at Barcelona, four years earlier.

Twenty-seventh of July, two thousand and eleven. Flamengo away at Santos. Santos have an eighteen-year-old prodigy in their starting eleven who is, at that point in his life, beginning to be discussed as the future of Brazilian football. Within thirty minutes, Santos lead three-nil. The eighteen-year-old has scored. The Maracanã press box, watching from afar, has begun to write a story about the symbolism of Neymar dismantling ron-al-DEEN-yo on his own pitch.

That is not the story that publishes.

ron-al-DEEN-yo, in the second half, scores from a free kick. Then sets up a goal. Then scores again. Then sets up the winner. Final score: Santos four, Flamengo five.

Hat-trick. Two assists. Three goals down at half-time, on the road, at thirty-one years old, against the best young footballer in Brazil. ron-al-DEEN-yo turned that match around almost single-handedly, and the global football press — which had spent the morning of the same day asking when he would announce retirement — wrote about Neymar.

He left Flamengo in May twenty-twelve, after a contractual dispute, having scored thirty-five goals in fifty-eight matches and won three regional championships. Four days later — four days — he signed for at-LEH-tee-koh mee-NAY-roo of Belo Horizonte.

BEH-loo oh-ree-ZON-tchee is not, in football terms, a glamour city. It is the third-largest city in Brazil. It has produced two great clubs — Cruzeiro, who at-LEH-tee-koh share a stadium with, and at-LEH-tee-koh themselves, who at the time of his signing had not won the Brazilian league in forty-one years and had never, in their one-hundred-and-seven-year history, won the Copa Libertadores.

ron-al-DEEN-yo's first season at the club, two thousand and twelve, ends with at-LEH-tee-koh in second place in the Brasileirão. They qualify for the Libertadores for the first time in five years. ron-al-DEEN-yo, in the same season, is named the best player in Brazil's domestic league. He wins the BOH-lah jee OH-roo. The Bola de Ouro. The award given annually to the best Brazilian footballer in the Brasileirão, voted by the Brazilian football press.

Thirty-two years old. Five years after his alleged decline began.

The award gets, internationally, two paragraphs of coverage. One in The Guardian. One in Marca. The European football press, which has spent two thousand and twelve writing about Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, Andrés Iniesta, and Andrea Pirlo, has decided that the Brazilian league is no longer a place where significance happens.

A continental trophy is about to disagree.

chapters.title: The Trophy That Counts
chapters.beat: 2013 Libertadores. The whole spine. Round of 16 vs São Paulo, 1-2 / 4-1 (Ronaldinho free kick the second leg). QF vs Tijuana 2-2 / 1-1 — advance away goals. SF vs Newell's: lose first leg 0-2 in Rosario; second leg at Mineirão: Ronaldinho scores 44', Tardelli equalises 88', penalties — Victor saves two. Ronaldinho photographed crying in centre circle. Final vs Olimpia: 0-2 in Asunción (94th-minute goal); 2-0 second leg at Mineirão (Tardelli + Jô); penalties 4-3. Atlético's first Libertadores in 115 years. 4 goals + 7 assists in tournament. Subscribe ask embedded at end.
chapters.narration:
The two-thousand-thirteen Libertadores. The most prestigious trophy in South American club football. A tournament played across two halves of an enormous continent, in altitudes that vary by three thousand metres, in stadiums where the home fans throw fireworks at the opposition team bus. A tournament that has been won, before two thousand and thirteen, by Pelé's Santos. By Maradona's Boca. By Ricardo Bochini's Independiente. By Romário's Vasco. The trophy of South American myth.

at-LEH-tee-koh mee-NAY-roo, in two thousand and thirteen, are entering the tournament for the first time in five years.

Their coach is a forty-nine-year-old Brazilian called KOO-kah, whose previous head-coaching stint had been at Cruzeiro, the city rivals. Their squad is, by South American standards, decent without being intimidating. There is a strong centre back called Réver. There is a forward called Jô, who Manchester City fans will remember without affection. There is, of course, ron-al-DEEN-yo Gaúcho, thirty-three years old, his hair tied back in the long ponytail that has by then been the subject of three thousand magazine covers.

The group stage they navigate without incident.

Then the knockout rounds begin.

Round of sixteen. at-LEH-tee-koh draw São Paulo. They lose the first leg, away, two-one. They win the second leg, at home, four-one. ron-al-DEEN-yo scores in the second leg from a free kick that crosses the goal line at a velocity their goalkeeper later admits he did not see leave the boot.

Quarter-final. They draw tee-WAH-nah, of all places. A Mexican club, in the Libertadores by virtue of CONMEBOL invitation, which Brazilian football media regards as an embarrassment. tee-WAH-nah, in their stadium up in northern Mexico, hold at-LEH-tee-koh to a one-one draw in the second leg. Aggregate three-three. at-LEH-tee-koh advance on away goals.

Semi-final. Newell's Old Boys. The Argentinian club where Lionel Messi spent his childhood. The first leg is in Rosario. Newell's win two-nil. ron-al-DEEN-yo, watching from the bench in the second half due to a thigh strain, is photographed afterwards looking — and the Argentinian press use this exact word — broken.

The second leg is at the Mineirão.

Two-nil down on aggregate. Bottom of every model. The Mineirão is at full capacity. The atmosphere has been described, by people who were there, as the loudest atmosphere in Brazilian club football this decade. ron-al-DEEN-yo, at thirty-three, has insisted on starting.

Forty-fourth minute. He scores from open play. Aggregate two-one.

Eighty-eighth minute. Diego Tardelli equalises on aggregate. Penalties.

ron-al-DEEN-yo scores his penalty. at-LEH-tee-koh's goalkeeper, Victor, saves two for Newell's. The shootout is won. The Mineirão stays at full volume for, by some accounts, twenty minutes after the final whistle. ron-al-DEEN-yo is photographed crying in the centre circle, kneeling, holding his head.

The image is reproduced, the next morning, in every Brazilian sports publication. It is reproduced in zero major European outlets.

The final is against Olimpia of Paraguay. oh-LEEM-pee-ah, who have won this tournament three times, are by every analytical model in two thousand and thirteen slight favourites. The first leg is in ah-soon-see-OWN. oh-LEEM-pee-ah win two-nil. The second goal arrives in the ninety-fourth minute.

The aggregate, returning to Belo Horizonte, is two-nil to Paraguay.

Twenty-fourth of July, two thousand and thirteen. The Mineirão, again, is at full capacity. Eighty-thousand-plus, by the official figure. The match begins.

Forty-seventh minute. ron-al-DEEN-yo takes a corner. The corner is met, by Diego Tardelli, on the volley. One-nil. Aggregate two-one.

Sixty-eighth minute. Jô heads a Diego Tardelli cross. Two-nil. Aggregate two-two.

Penalties.

ron-al-DEEN-yo scores his penalty. Victor, the goalkeeper, saves oh-LEEM-pee-ah's second. at-LEH-tee-koh win the shootout, four-three, on a penalty by Leandro Donizete.

at-LEH-tee-koh mee-NAY-roo are champions of South America. For the first time in their one-hundred-and-fifteen-year history.

ron-al-DEEN-yo, at thirty-three, with four goals and seven assists across the tournament, is named the official Best Player of the Libertadores. He is photographed, that evening, lifting the trophy in front of a Mineirão that has refused to leave the stadium for three hours after the final whistle.

The next morning's European football coverage is dominated by Bayern Munich's pre-season tour and Arsenal's transfer activity.

If you've made it this far and you're realising you wrote off a player who was still winning continental trophies in his thirties — and the algorithm only knows you're still here if you tell it — subscribe. We do this kind of football reckoning twice a month. The next one is going to be a player you definitely have wrong right now.

chapters.title: The Country That Cried For Him
chapters.beat: Summer 2014: bonus dispute leaves Atlético. Major European clubs decline. Brazilian clubs decline. Signs for Querétaro of Liga MX, 5 Sept 2014. The 'novelty signing' framing. First goal vs Chiapas free kick. April 2015 — Estadio Azteca, Querétaro 4-0 Club América. Two Ronaldinho goals (23' free kick, 72' half-volley). Standing ovation from América fans. Ronaldinho visibly tearing up. The moment becomes Mexican football folklore. Liga MX final vs Santos Laguna — lost 5-3 agg, but Querétaro's first ever final. Ronaldinho 8 goals + 7 assists.
chapters.narration:
Twelve months after the Libertadores. Summer two thousand and fourteen. ron-al-DEEN-yo is, again, a free agent. at-LEH-tee-koh mee-NAY-roo and the player have separated after a bonus dispute. He is thirty-four. He has, by any rational calendar of a footballer's career, two seasons left.

Major European clubs, asked publicly whether they will sign him, decline. Brazilian clubs, asked privately, decline. The conventional next move for a Brazilian footballer of his age and pedigree is the United Arab Emirates or Saudi Arabia. The money is there. The football is not. The career terminates politely.

ron-al-DEEN-yo signs for keh-REH-tah-roh.

keh-REH-tah-roh are a Mexican club. They play in Mexico's first division, Liga MX. Their nickname is GAH-yos BLAHN-kos — the White Roosters. Their stadium, La Corregidora, holds thirty-three thousand. They have, in their then-sixty-five-year history, never won the Mexican league. They have, in fact, never been to a Mexican league final.

The signing is, by international football media's calculation, a curiosity. A novelty. A pre-retirement holiday. ESPN runs a single column on it. The European outlets that bother to mention the move file it under transfer news from emerging markets.

Then, again, ron-al-DEEN-yo plays.

His first goal for keh-REH-tah-roh, against Chiapas, is a free kick from thirty yards that the Mexican commentator describes as something he has not seen in his country in fifteen years. His third goal arrives in his fifth match. By the end of the Apertura tournament, his half-season debut, he has three goals, an assist, and the highest passing-accuracy figure of any attacking midfielder in the league.

He is thirty-four years old.

In April two thousand and fifteen, keh-REH-tah-roh travel to Mexico City to play Club América. ah-MEH-ree-kah are Mexico's biggest club, the league's reigning champions, the team that almost every neutral Mexican fan loves to hate but that nearly every Mexican casual fan supports anyway. The match is at the ess-TAH-dee-oh az-TEH-kah. The same stadium where Maradona scored the goal of the century in nineteen-eighty-six. The same stadium where Pelé's Brazil scored four against Italy in nineteen-seventy. A venue that, by Mexican football logic, is hostile to ah-MEH-ree-kah's opponents the way Old Trafford is hostile to Manchester United's.

In the twenty-third minute, ron-al-DEEN-yo scores from a free kick. In the seventy-second, he scores again — a half-volley from twenty yards.

The Mexican broadcast, in real time, captures the response from the home end behind the goal.

The ah-MEH-ree-kah fans applaud. Not after the match. Not after the second goal lands. As ron-al-DEEN-yo turns away from his second goal, with his arms raised, the home fans, in their own stadium, watching their own club lose four-nil at home, applaud the man scoring against them.

ron-al-DEEN-yo, on the broadcast, can be seen — and Mexican Twitter, the next morning, will replay this segment ten million times — visibly tearing up as he runs back to his half. He kisses his shirt. He waves at the home crowd. The home crowd applauds louder.

This moment, the standing ovation at the az-TEH-kah, is, in Mexican football culture, considered one of the great moments of the modern Liga MX era. It is referenced in books. It is referenced in podcasts. It is referenced, every year on its anniversary, by every major Mexican sports outlet.

It receives, in the English-language football press, a single Bleacher Report listicle.

ron-al-DEEN-yo finishes the season with eight goals, seven assists, and a Liga MX final appearance. keh-REH-tah-roh, the team that had never been to a Mexican league final in their sixty-five-year history, lose to Santos Laguna five-three on aggregate. ron-al-DEEN-yo, in the second leg, scores. He is thirty-five years old. He has, in his late-career third act, just taken a Mexican club to the highest peak in its institutional history.

The European football press, that summer, is preoccupied with Lionel Messi's Champions League victory and Cristiano Ronaldo's contract renewal at Real Madrid. The phrase 'where is ron-al-DEEN-yo now,' that summer, is a Google search trend.

He was, in fact, in az-TEH-kah.

chapters.title: We Were the Ones Who Lost
chapters.beat: The reframe. 8 trophies between 2008-2015. 100+ goals. Best player of three different continental leagues across that span. The audience changed, not him. Premier League broadcast money tripled. La Liga ascendancy. Serie A faded from non-Italian view. Brazilian league not watched in Europe. Mexican league never watched in Europe. The decline was geographical, not athletic. Receipts beat: 'pull up an article from 2010 calling him finished, then pull up the trophy he lifted that year' — invite the audience to verify.
chapters.narration:
The story, taken together, is not the story we were told.

Between two thousand and eight and two thousand and fifteen — the seven-year period football media collectively designated ron-al-DEEN-yo's decline — he won eight major trophies. Four in Brazil. One in South America. Three in the Italian cup competitions. He scored over a hundred goals. He registered over eighty assists. He was named the best player in three different leagues across two continents in a span of three years.

In the same seven years, he played for four clubs. He was the headline signing for each of them. He was, in three out of the four, named player of the season at least once.

These are not the numbers of a player in decline. They are the numbers of a player whose audience changed.

The audience, between two thousand and seven and two thousand and eight, did change. Football's economic centre of gravity moved. The Premier League's broadcast money tripled in the decade after Sky's first deal. La Liga's ascendancy under Messi and Cristiano absorbed the world's attention. Serie A, the league that defined the early careers of every great player of the twentieth century, was, by two thousand and ten, no longer a league anyone outside Italy watched closely. Brazilian football, the cradle of every great Brazilian player ever exported, was, by two thousand and eleven, watched in Europe by a small specialist press. Mexican football, in any honest accounting, has never been watched in Europe at all.

So when we, the European-and-North-American football audience, said ron-al-DEEN-yo had declined — what we actually meant was that he was no longer playing in front of us.

Those two facts are not the same fact.

ron-al-DEEN-yo, between thirty and thirty-five, was a top-tier footballer playing top-tier football. He was just doing it in markets we had decided not to watch. The decline was, geographically, real. The player was not in our line of sight. But our line of sight is not the world. And the trophies he won, in the leagues we had stopped watching, were heavier than what most of his peers won during the same window in the leagues we did.

If you doubt any of this — and you should, scepticism is healthy — try this. Stop the video. Pull up an article from May twenty thirteen, the week of the Atlético Mineiro Libertadores final. Pick any major English-language outlet. Search for the word 'finished.' Search for the phrase 'past it.' Then pull up the photographs from the next morning, of ron-al-DEEN-yo lifting that trophy at the Mineirão.

Notice the dates.

Then pull up an article from October twenty-fifteen, six months after the az-TEH-kah ovation. Search the same outlet, sometimes the same byline, for the word 'forgotten.' For the phrase 'wasted.' Notice the dates again.

The articles do not retract. They do not correct. They do not even acknowledge that the player they were calling finished in twenty-thirteen had, between then and the article calling him forgotten in twenty-fifteen, taken two clubs to silverware in two countries.

The Bola de Ouro. The Copa Libertadores. The Carioca championship — twice. The Campeonato Mineiro — twice. A Liga MX final at thirty-five. A pre-game ovation at the az-TEH-kah. He won.

We weren't there.

That isn't his story. That's our story. ron-al-DEEN-yo, the actual man, the actual footballer, played joyful, decorated, attendance-shattering football into his mid-thirties. The thing that was lost, in those seven years, was not him.

The thing that was lost was us watching.

chapters.beat: Direct address. Retired 2018 at 38. The Real Madrid 2018 hall-of-fame opponent induction + same-week Querétaro testimonial. Two crowds, four thousand miles apart, treat him as the same player. The 'two halves' content shape that media keeps making — Barcelona half + 'wasted potential' half. Reframe: there was no waste. The comments-bait CTA — who's the next Ronaldinho.
chapters.narration:
ron-al-DEEN-yo officially retired in twenty eighteen. He was thirty-eight. The retirement statement was published, in Portuguese, by his brother, who served throughout his career as his agent. The statement was, by football-retirement-statement standards, brief.

He played the second half of his retirement testimonial in keh-REH-tah-roh, in front of thirty thousand Mexican fans, in the same week he had been formally honoured as one of Real Madrid's greatest opposition players ever to play at the bare-na-BAY-oo. Both crowds, separated by four thousand miles, treated him as the same player. Because, by every measurable footballing metric, he was the same player.

It was the audience that had been two different audiences.

Football media, since his retirement, has produced an enormous amount of ron-al-DEEN-yo content. The shape of the content is consistent. It is, almost without exception, a story of two halves: the Barcelona half — bare-na-BAY-oo standing ovation, Ballon d'Or, World Player of the Year — and the post-Barcelona half, in which the narrator's voice goes soft and the editing slows down and the phrase that always emerges is something about wasted potential.

There was no wasted potential.

There was a player who continued to play, continued to win, continued to be loved by audiences who had access to him. There was a press class that decided, around two thousand and eight, that he had ended his career, and that has, ever since, refused to update.

So here is the question this video is built around. Here is the comments section.

Who's the player you've stopped watching because he's playing in a league you don't follow? Whose career do you assume has ended because you can't see it on Sky Sports or TNT? The Brazilian thirty-something nobody outside São Paulo is talking about. The Argentine playmaker tearing up the MLS. The veteran in the Saudi Pro League the European press has agreed, by silence, doesn't count.

Who's the next ron-al-DEEN-yo?

Drop a name. I'll pin the best argument.
